clinical_knowledge.topic: Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: High detrusor storage pressures and poor compliance can cause reflux, hydronephrosis, recurrent infection, and renal deterioration.

In people with spinal cord injury at or above T6, autonomic dysreflexia is a hypertensive emergency; sit the patient upright, remove tight clothing, identify and relieve triggers such as bladder obstruction, and seek emergency care.
Use urinalysis and culture only when symptoms or systemic features suggest infection; bacteriuria or cloudy urine alone is common with catheterization and should not prompt antibiotics.

Clean intermittent catheterization and pressure-lowering therapy are individualized. Botulinum toxin can improve storage but may worsen retention, so ability to catheterize and follow-up are essential.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: incontinence, urinary tract infections, and autonomic dysreflexia in paraplegic patient with high bladder pressures
T6 paraplegia, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, poor compliance, and storage pressure above 40 cm H2O place upper tracts at risk.
Measure blood pressure during symptoms, assess catheter patency and residuals, renal function, and upper-tract surveillance.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Missing autonomic dysreflexia, severe hypertension, retention, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, or acute kidney injury.
Giving botulinum toxin without confirming a safe catheterization plan and renal-aware follow-up.
management_principles: Urgently assess and treat autonomic dysreflexia or sepsis; check drainage immediately when bladder distension is suspected.
Refer to neuro-urology for pressure-lowering strategy, catheterization review, renal ultrasound/creatinine surveillance, and repeat urodynamics when indicated.
Culture and treat symptomatic infection based on results, renal function, and local guidance; avoid routine suppressive antibiotics.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury: incontinence, urinary tract infections, and autonomic dysreflexia in paraplegic patient with high bladder pressures. 39M with T6 paraplegia presenting with urinary leakage between self-catheterizations where urodynamics reveal detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, poor bladder compliance, and elevated detrusor storage pressures (>40 cmH2O) requiring intradetrusor OnabotulinumtoxinA injections.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Neurogenic Bladder Spinal Cord Injury.
reference_soap.assessment: High-risk neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction from T6 injury with dangerous storage pressures and autonomic dysreflexia risk.
reference_soap.plan: Check blood pressure and bladder drainage now if dysreflexia symptoms occur; arrange urgent neuro-urology management to protect renal function. Treat only symptomatic, culture-supported infection and individualize pressure-lowering treatment.

teaching.diagnosis: High-risk neurogenic bladder due to spinal cord injury
teaching.one_liner: A man with T6 paraplegia has dyssynergia, poor compliance, and high storage pressures, creating renal and autonomic dysreflexia risk.
differentials: Bladder outlet obstruction from catheter malposition
Autonomic dysreflexia from another trigger (bowel impaction, skin ulcer)

must_ask.say: How often do you self-catheterize each day, and has that schedule changed recently?
Do you get pounding headaches, sweating, or flushing above your level of injury when your bladder is full?
Are you leaking urine between catheterizations, and how much?
Have you had repeated bladder infections, cloudy urine, or fevers?

must_ask.objective: Level and completeness of spinal cord injury
must_ask.say: Can you remind me the level of your spinal cord injury and whether it's complete or incomplete?
